title: Nickel Mines
hook: in 2006 an Amish community in Pennsylvania publicly forgave the man who shot their children, and comforted his family

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ravensbrück, and a hand held out in a Munich church. Your line was hard, and possible. Which hard thing did you let yourself name? Today, the last of the Christian voices this block, and a whole community facing the hardest forgiveness. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

Nickel Mines is a small place in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, with farms, buggies and a one-room Amish schoolhouse. One autumn morning, a man from the area, not Amish, walked into that school with guns and shot girls in their classroom, and then himself. This lesson won't linger on the details. What it remembers is what came next. Within hours, Amish neighbors went to the gunman's family. Not to accuse. To comfort them. Today: Nickel Mines.
screen: `A ONE-ROOM SCHOOLHOUSE.` → `A MORNING OF GRIEF.` → `NEIGHBORS GO TO HIS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: This account follows the book Amish Grace, written by scholars who studied the community's response. First, the visits. The book describes Amish neighbors going to the gunman's widow and his parents in the first days, to say they held no grudge, and to sit with them. Amish neighbors, it says, were among the mourners at his burial, standing with the family of the man who had done this. Second, the gifts. Gifts of money came in for the Amish families. The book tells how the community shared some of it with the gunman's widow and children, who had lost someone too and had done nothing wrong. Those are the other family. Third, where it came from. The authors trace the response to the Lord's Prayer, which the book describes as prayed daily in Amish homes, and to Jesus's words right after it in Matthew: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." The same line these Christian voices began with. For the people of Nickel Mines, in the book's telling, that verse wasn't a nice idea. It was something you do, even here. Fourth, what forgiveness didn't mean. The book is careful about this. The families grieved, deeply and for a long time. Forgiving didn't erase the loss, or call what happened anything but evil. It meant giving up the right to revenge, and refusing to let bitterness take over. Some outsiders praised it; some questioned whether it came too fast. The authors take both reactions seriously. What's left is a plain picture: grieving parents sitting with a widow, remembering that the man who did this also left behind a family.
screen: `NEIGHBORS AT HIS FAMILY'S DOOR.` · `GIFTS SHARED WITH HIS WIDOW.` · `IF YE FORGIVE MEN THEIR TRESPASSES.` · `GRIEF STAYS. REVENGE GOES.` · then, large: `THE OTHER FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Before anything else, take a few slow breaths. This practice is gentle on purpose. Think of someone who has caused harm, close to you or far off in the news. Don't focus on them. Turn instead to the people around them: a parent, a partner, a child. People who didn't choose what happened, and who carry it anyway. Picture one of them at a kitchen table, alone with it. Let a small wish rise for that person: some peace, some company, someone at the door. If you pray, you can hold that family in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Nickel Mines. The Amish community in Pennsylvania that, after a shooting at its school, went to comfort the gunman's family. Today's word.
Your line: the other family. Today, when you hear of someone who did harm, give one thought to the people who love them and are carrying it too. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Amish Christians pray the Lord's Prayer and take its line about forgiving others as something to practice; in the book Amish Grace, Amish people interviewed describe forgiveness as giving up revenge, not forgetting the loss.

fork.setup: your community has just suffered something terrible, and the man who did it is dead. his widow and children live nearby. what does the Amish community do, in the book's account?
options: stay away from his family entirely.
go to his family to comfort them.
ask the town to move them away.
fork.reveal: they went to his family within hours, to say they held no grudge, and later shared gifts with his widow and children.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Amish forgave and moved on.
what it means: grieving families gave up revenge and went to comfort the family of the man who harmed them.
what a scholar hears: the authors of Amish Grace trace it to a daily habit: the Lord's Prayer, and Matthew 6:14–15 read as something to do.
